title: The Skin That Paints Itself
paragraphs: An octopus resting on a patch of weed can be invisible until it moves, and then it is simply there, a pale animal jetting away from what looked like bare algae.
Aristotle noticed the trick more than two thousand years ago, writing that the octopus changes its color to resemble the stones around it.
A chameleon or a flounder takes seconds to minutes to shift its color; a cuttlefish can switch its entire body pattern in under a second.
The system behind this belongs to the coleoid cephalopods, the octopuses, cuttlefishes, and squids, and not to their shelled relative the nautilus.
The engine of the change is the chromatophore, a word that means something different here than in a fish or a frog.
In those vertebrates a chromatophore is a single cell that darkens or pales by moving pigment granules within itself, a process that takes seconds to minutes and is often driven by hormones.

In a cephalopod a chromatophore is a small organ: an elastic sac of yellow, orange, red, brown, or black pigment ringed by radial muscle fibers, usually fifteen to twenty-five of them, attached like the spokes of a wheel.
When the fibers contract they pull the sac outward into a flat disc, spreading the pigment into view; when they relax, the sac's own elasticity snaps it back to a dot.
Fully opened, a chromatophore in a large octopus can be more than a millimeter across; retracted, it is nearly invisible.
What makes the organ fast is the wiring.

Each radial muscle is driven directly by motor neurons whose cell bodies lie in the chromatophore lobes of the brain, so a decision made there reaches the skin along a nerve, with no hormone in the loop.
Cut the nerve to a patch of skin and the patch goes pale and still, its chromatophores slack while the skin around it keeps flickering.
An adult common octopus carries on the order of a million of these organs, and the brain drives them in groups, so the skin holds a repertoire of patterns rather than a photograph.
The British zoologist John Messenger summarized the system in a 2001 review that remains a standard reference, and I know of no better example of a nervous system reaching the surface of the body.
Pigment alone cannot produce the blues and greens that cuttlefish and squid display; no chromatophore holds a blue pigment.

Those colors come from a layer of cells beneath the chromatophores called iridophores, each holding stacks of thin plates of a protein called reflectin, identified in 2004 in the Hawaiian bobtail squid.
Light reflecting from the successive plates interferes with itself, canceling some wavelengths and reinforcing others, so the color depends on the spacing of the plates rather than on any pigment.
In some squid the spacing is adjustable: the nerve transmitter acetylcholine makes the reflectin condense, shifting the reflected color toward the blue over several seconds.
A third cell type, the leucophore, scatters all wavelengths about equally, so it looks white in white light, yellowish under yellow light, and takes on whatever color the surroundings supply.
Leucophores are generally thought to be passive, though a few squid can switch theirs on and off, and the matter is not settled.
The patterns the animals produce with all this equipment are not infinite.

Working with the European cuttlefish, Roger Hanlon and his colleagues sorted its body patterns into three classes: uniform, evenly light or dark; mottle, a scatter of small light and dark patches; and disruptive, a few large, high-contrast components that break the body's outline into pieces that do not add up to an animal.
The best-known disruptive component is the white square, a pale patch on the mantle.

Hanlon's group, at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Massachusetts, placed cuttlefish on checkerboards and found that they produced disruptive patterns when the checks were roughly the size of their own white square, and other patterns when the checks were much smaller.
The animal, in other words, measures the scene and selects a pattern from a limited set rather than copying what it sees.
Here the story runs into a puzzle that has occupied biologists for half a century.
Cephalopod camouflage looks colored, and to a diver it often seems to match the hue of sand or weed, yet the eyes that direct it appear to be color-blind.

Color vision in the usual sense requires at least two kinds of photoreceptor tuned to different wavelengths, so the brain can compare their responses, and the retinas of almost every cephalopod examined contain a single visual pigment.

In 1977 Messenger reported that octopuses could learn to tell a brighter target from a dimmer one but not two colors apart, and in 1996 he and Justin Marshall showed that cuttlefish on backgrounds of two colors matched in brightness responded as if the backgrounds were plain.
The only clear exception found so far is the firefly squid, a small bioluminescent species of Japanese waters that carries three visual pigments and lives in open water rather than on a seabed.
The first explanation is that the match is less exact than it looks.
The leucophores and iridophores reflect whatever light reaches them, so a cuttlefish on yellow sand under yellowish light returns yellow from its skin without having to see it.

Spectral measurements of cuttlefish on natural backgrounds have generally found the match good but not perfect, and for a fish searching a seabed a mismatch in brightness or pattern is probably far more revealing than one in hue.
I think this explanation carries much of the weight, but a passive reflector can only return the light it is given, and the chromatophores laid over it still have to be the right colors.

In 2016 Alexander Stubbs, a graduate student at the University of California, Berkeley, and his father Christopher Stubbs, a Harvard physicist, proposed a bolder idea: that cephalopods might extract color from a flaw most eyes suppress.
A lens bends blue light more strongly than red, so the two come to focus at slightly different distances, an effect called chromatic aberration.
The odd pupils of cephalopods, the W shape of the cuttlefish and the horizontal slot of the octopus, admit light through the edges of the lens rather than its center, which worsens the aberration.
Their calculations showed that an animal with a single pigment could in principle work out an object's color by noting the focus setting at which it becomes sharp.

The idea is elegant, and it would explain why an animal keeps a pupil shape that costs it sharpness, but it remains a calculation: no one has yet shown a cuttlefish doing it, and I would hold the hypothesis loosely until someone does.
A third line of evidence moves the question from the eye to the skin.

In 2015 Desmond Ramirez and Todd Oakley showed that patches of skin cut from the California two-spot octopus expand their chromatophores when light falls on them, with no eye or brain attached, and that the skin contains the same opsin, or light-catching protein, found in the retina.
The response is slow, taking seconds, and because the skin uses the one pigment the eye uses, it cannot by itself add color discrimination; what it may add is local information about brightness.
Cephalopods also detect the polarization of light, which we cannot see at all, and which gives them another channel of contrast underwater.
Whether any of these channels combine into something like color vision is unknown; the honest summary is that the animals produce colored camouflage by means we do not fully understand.
What is certain is simpler than any of these hypotheses.

The chromatophore is a muscle-driven organ wired straight to the brain; the reflecting cells beneath it supply the colors pigment cannot; the brain selects patterns by the size and contrast of what it sees; and all of this happens in less than a second.
The rest, the question of how a color-blind animal paints itself to suit a colored world, is open, and I would rather leave it open than close it with a tidy answer the evidence does not yet support.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a chromatophore in a fish or a frog differs from one in a cephalopod in that the vertebrate chromatophore
choices: is a small organ whose pigment sac is pulled open by a ring of muscles
contains a blue pigment that cephalopod chromatophores lack
is a single cell that moves pigment granules within itself
changes color in a fraction of a second under direct nerve control
reflects light from stacked plates rather than holding any pigment

proof.quote: a chromatophore is a single cell that darkens or pales by moving pigment granules within itself

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says that in fish and frogs a chromatophore is a single cell that darkens or pales by moving pigment granules within itself, and then contrasts that with the cephalopod version, which is a small organ.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 2 describes the muscle-ringed sac as the cephalopod chromatophore, not the vertebrate one.
Contradicted: paragraph 4 says no chromatophore holds a blue pigment.
Reversed: speed and direct nerve control are what paragraph 3 attributes to the cephalopod organ.
Wrong cell type: stacked reflecting plates belong to the iridophores of paragraph 4.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the pigment in a cephalopod chromatophore comes into view when
choices: radial muscle fibers contract and pull the elastic sac into a flat disc
the elastic sac relaxes and snaps outward into a dot
hormones carried in the blood signal the sac to release its granules
acetylcholine makes the pigment inside the sac condense
the muscle fibers relax and allow the sac to spread under its own elasticity

proof.quote: When the fibers contract they pull the sac outward into a flat disc, spreading the pigment into view

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says that when the fibers contract they pull the sac outward into a flat disc, spreading the pigment into view; relaxing does the opposite.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the dot is the retracted state, which the sac snaps back to when the fibers relax.
Wrong mechanism: hormones are tied to the vertebrate chromatophore in paragraph 2, and paragraph 3 says there is no hormone in the loop.
Wrong cell: acetylcholine acts on reflectin in iridophores, in paragraph 4.
Reversed: paragraph 2 says relaxation lets the sac's elasticity pull it back to a dot, not spread it.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that if the radial muscles of a cephalopod's chromatophores were temporarily paralyzed, the animal's skin would most likely
choices: darken, since the pigment sacs would spread without resistance
keep its current pattern frozen in place until the muscles recovered
shift toward blue as the iridophores took over
turn pale, since each sac would retract on its own
flicker more rapidly as the brain tried to restore control

proof.quote: when they relax, the sac's own elasticity snaps it back to a dot
the patch goes pale and still, its chromatophores slack

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says the sac retracts on its own elasticity whenever the fibers relax, and paragraph 3 shows what that looks like when the nerve is cut: the patch goes pale and still. Paralyzed muscles cannot contract, so every sac would retract.
distractorNotes: Reversed: spreading requires the muscles to contract; without them the sacs retract.
Contradicted: the sac does not hold its shape on its own; paragraph 2 says elasticity snaps it back to a dot.
Unrelated: nothing in the passage says iridophores compensate when chromatophores fail.
Contradicted: paragraph 3 says a patch without working control goes still, not more active.

questions.stem: The author mentions cutting the nerve to a patch of skin in paragraph 3 primarily to
choices: warn that the chromatophore system is easily damaged
show that the chromatophores depend on direct control from the brain
explain why an adult octopus needs so many chromatophores
introduce the role of hormones in regulating the skin's pattern
describe how scientists first counted the organs in a single patch of skin

proof.quote: a decision made there reaches the skin along a nerve, with no hormone in the loop
Cut the nerve to a patch of skin and the patch goes pale and still

questions.why: Paragraph 3 is about the wiring: the brain reaches the skin along a nerve with no hormone in the loop. The cut-nerve example demonstrates that dependence, since the patch stops working the moment its nerve is gone.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: the author never says the system is fragile; the example is about control, not damage.
Wrong detail: the million-organ count comes later in the paragraph and is not explained by the nerve cut.
Reversed: the same paragraph says there is no hormone in the loop.
Outside the passage: no counting method is described.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the color produced by an iridophore depends on
choices: which of the five pigments its elastic sac contains
how brightly the water around the animal is lit
the number of radial muscle fibers attached around it
the opsin it shares with the animal's retina
the spacing of its stacked plates of reflectin

proof.quote: the color depends on the spacing of the plates rather than on any pigment

questions.why: Paragraph 4 says light reflecting from the successive plates interferes with itself, so the color depends on the spacing of the plates rather than on any pigment.
distractorNotes: Wrong cell: the five pigments and the elastic sac belong to the chromatophore in paragraph 2.
Wrong cell: taking on the surrounding light is what paragraph 4 says the leucophore does.
Wrong cell: radial muscles ring the chromatophore sac, not the iridophore.
Wrong paragraph: the shared opsin is in the skin study of paragraph 9 and has nothing to do with iridophore color.

questions.stem: According to the passage, each of the following is true of iridophores EXCEPT:
choices: They hold a blue pigment that the chromatophores lack.
They lie in a layer beneath the chromatophores.
Their plates are built from a protein called reflectin.
They produce the blues and greens that pigment cannot.
In some squid their color shifts over several seconds.

proof.quote: a layer of cells beneath the chromatophores called iridophores
stacks of thin plates of a protein called reflectin
Those colors come from a layer of cells beneath the chromatophores called iridophores
shifting the reflected color toward the blue over several seconds
the color depends on the spacing of the plates rather than on any pigment

questions.why: Paragraph 4 says iridophore color depends on the spacing of the plates rather than on any pigment, and the paragraph opens by saying no chromatophore holds a blue pigment either. The other four statements are all in paragraph 4.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 4, sentence 2 places iridophores in a layer beneath the chromatophores.
Paragraph 4, sentence 2 says the plates are made of a protein called reflectin.
Paragraph 4 opens by saying pigment cannot make the blues and greens and that those colors come from the iridophores.
Paragraph 4, sentence 4 says the reflected color shifts toward the blue over several seconds in some squid.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a cuttlefish leucophore viewed under blue light would most likely appear
choices: white, because it scatters every wavelength about equally
dark, because it absorbs the blue light it cannot reflect
bluish, because it takes on the color of the light reaching it
yellowish, because its stacked plates condense in blue light
red, because blue light is reinforced and the other colors canceled

proof.quote: it looks white in white light, yellowish under yellow light, and takes on whatever color the surroundings supply

questions.why: Paragraph 4 says a leucophore looks white in white light, yellowish under yellow light, and takes on whatever color the surroundings supply. Run that rule with blue light and the cell looks bluish.
distractorNotes: Half right: it does scatter all wavelengths equally, but that is exactly why it returns the color it is given, and the light given here is blue.
Reversed: paragraph 4 says the leucophore scatters light, not that it absorbs it.
Wrong cell and wrong light: condensing plates belong to the iridophore, and yellow comes from yellow light.
Wrong cell: canceling and reinforcing wavelengths is the iridophore mechanism, and it would not turn blue light red.

questions.stem: According to the passage, cuttlefish placed on checkerboards produced disruptive patterns when
choices: the checks were a great deal smaller than the animal's own white square
the checks were roughly the size of the animal's white square
the board was uniformly light or uniformly dark in tone
the checks were in two colors matched for brightness
the board was lit from above by yellowish light

proof.quote: they produced disruptive patterns when the checks were roughly the size of their own white square

questions.why: Paragraph 5 says Hanlon's group found disruptive patterns when the checks were roughly the size of the animal's own white square, and other patterns when the checks were much smaller.
distractorNotes: Reversed: much smaller checks produced other patterns, according to paragraph 5.
Wrong detail: a uniform board is not described; uniform is one of the animal's pattern classes.
Wrong paragraph: brightness-matched colors are the 1996 color-blindness test in paragraph 6, where the animals responded as if the board were plain.
Outside the passage: yellowish light appears in paragraph 7 and has nothing to do with checkerboards.

questions.stem: Which new situation best illustrates the principle described in the last sentence of paragraph 5?
choices: A photocopier reproduces a document line by line so that the copy matches the original exactly
A painter mixes a fresh shade for every patch of sky until the canvas matches the view
A mirror shows whatever object is placed in front of it, in every detail
A musician with three songs picks the one whose tempo fits the mood of the room
A student memorizes a list of answers and repeats them regardless of the question

proof.quote: measures the scene and selects a pattern from a limited set rather than copying what it sees
The patterns the animals produce with all this equipment are not infinite.

questions.why: The rule in paragraph 5 is that the animal measures the scene and selects from a limited set rather than copying. A musician who reads the room and picks one of three songs is doing the same thing: measuring, then choosing from a small repertoire.
distractorNotes: Reversed: a photocopier copies exactly, which is what the passage says the animal does not do.
Reversed: mixing a new shade for every patch is copying with an unlimited palette, not selecting from a limited set.
Reversed: a mirror copies the scene; it makes no selection at all.
Half right: the set is limited, but the student ignores the scene instead of measuring it.

questions.stem: The author mentions the firefly squid in paragraph 6 primarily to
choices: offer evidence that cephalopod camouflage relies on bioluminescent light
show that color vision is common among squid that live in open water
introduce the species used in the 1996 brightness experiments
argue that the puzzle of color-blind camouflage has been solved
note an exception to the claim that cephalopods have one pigment

proof.quote: The only clear exception found so far is the firefly squid
the retinas of almost every cephalopod examined contain a single visual pigment

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says almost every cephalopod examined has a single visual pigment, then calls the firefly squid the only clear exception found so far. It is there to qualify the generalization honestly, not to overturn it.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: the squid's bioluminescence is mentioned in passing and never tied to camouflage.
Too strong: the passage calls it the only clear exception, not a common case.
Wrong species: the 1996 experiments in paragraph 6 used cuttlefish.
Reversed: paragraphs 9 and 10 say the puzzle remains open.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Messenger's 1977 experiments showed that octopuses
choices: learned to tell a brighter target from a dimmer one but not two colors apart
could be trained to distinguish two colors but not two levels of brightness
produced disruptive patterns only when the checks matched their white square
treated backgrounds of two colors matched in brightness as though they were plain backgrounds
expanded their chromatophores when light was shone on patches of their skin

proof.quote: octopuses could learn to tell a brighter target from a dimmer one but not two colors apart

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says that in 1977 Messenger reported octopuses could learn to tell a brighter target from a dimmer one but not two colors apart.
distractorNotes: Reversed: brightness was learnable and color was not.
Wrong paragraph and wrong animal: the checkerboard work in paragraph 5 was done with cuttlefish by Hanlon's group.
Wrong experiment: that is the 1996 cuttlefish result with Justin Marshall, later in the same sentence.
Wrong paragraph: the skin-and-light finding is the 2015 work of Ramirez and Oakley in paragraph 9.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 6, the word 'plain' most nearly means
choices: simple to understand
unattractive
honest and direct
unpatterned
obvious at a glance

proof.quote: responded as if the backgrounds were plain

questions.why: Paragraph 6 contrasts a background of two colors with one the cuttlefish treated as plain: the animals could not see the difference between the squares, so to them the board had no pattern. Plain here means unpatterned.
distractorNotes: This is the everyday sense of plain speech or a plain explanation, but a background is not something the cuttlefish understands.
Plain can mean homely, but the sentence is about what the cuttlefish could see, not about looks.
Plain speaking is another common meaning, and nothing in the sentence involves honesty.
Reversed: the point is that the two colors were not obvious to the animal at all.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a fish hunting over a seabed would be most likely to notice a cuttlefish whose
choices: hue differed slightly from the sand beneath it
brightness or pattern differed from the background
leucophores reflected the color of the surrounding light
chromatophores were the right colors for the place
iridophores had shifted toward the blue over several seconds

proof.quote: for a fish searching a seabed a mismatch in brightness or pattern is probably far more revealing than one in hue

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says that for a fish searching a seabed, a mismatch in brightness or pattern is probably far more revealing than one in hue. So a brightness or pattern mismatch is what would give the cuttlefish away.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 7 says a hue mismatch is the less revealing kind.
Reversed: reflecting the surrounding light is part of how the match is made, not how it fails.
Reversed: the right colors would help the cuttlefish hide, not expose it.
Unrelated: the iridophore color shift in paragraph 4 is not connected to being noticed.

questions.stem: All of the following are stated in the passage about the Stubbs hypothesis EXCEPT:
choices: It was proposed in 2016 by a graduate student and his physicist father.
It relies on chromatic aberration, the lens's unequal bending of colors.
It would account for a pupil shape that costs the animal sharpness.
It rests on calculations rather than on observed behavior.
It has been confirmed by tests with cuttlefish in the laboratory.

proof.quote: In 2016 Alexander Stubbs, a graduate student at the University of California, Berkeley, and his father Christopher Stubbs, a Harvard physicist, proposed
A lens bends blue light more strongly than red, so the two come to focus at slightly different distances, an effect called chromatic aberration.
it would explain why an animal keeps a pupil shape that costs it sharpness
it remains a calculation
no one has yet shown a cuttlefish doing it

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says the idea remains a calculation and that no one has yet shown a cuttlefish doing it, so it has not been confirmed. The other four statements are all in paragraph 8.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 8, sentence 1 gives the year, the graduate student, and his physicist father.
Paragraph 8, sentence 2 defines chromatic aberration as the lens bending blue more strongly than red.
Paragraph 8, sentence 5 says the idea would explain why an animal keeps a pupil shape that costs it sharpness.
Paragraph 8, sentence 5 says it remains a calculation, with no cuttlefish yet shown doing it.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the Stubbs hypothesis is best described as
choices: openly dismissive
entirely convinced
admiring but unconvinced
indifferent to its outcome
puzzled by its reasoning

proof.quote: The idea is elegant
I would hold the hypothesis loosely until someone does

questions.why: Paragraph 8 calls the idea elegant and credits what it would explain, then says it remains a calculation and that the author would hold it loosely until someone shows a cuttlefish doing it. That is admiration paired with reserved judgment.
distractorNotes: Too strong: an author who calls an idea elegant is not dismissing it.
Reversed: the author explicitly withholds belief until there is behavioral evidence.
Wrong register: the author cares enough to weigh the idea and say what would settle it.
Wrong register: the author lays out the reasoning clearly and finds it elegant, not confusing.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Ramirez and Oakley found that patches of skin from the California two-spot octopus
choices: turned pale and still as soon as their nerve supply was cut away
expanded their chromatophores in light with no eye or brain attached
contained an opsin that differed from the one found in the animal's retina
could tell colors apart even though the animal's retina could not
responded to light within a fraction of a second, faster than the eye does

proof.quote: expand their chromatophores when light falls on them, with no eye or brain attached

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says the skin patches expand their chromatophores when light falls on them, with no eye or brain attached, and that they contain the same opsin found in the retina.
distractorNotes: Wrong paragraph: the cut-nerve observation is in paragraph 3 and is not credited to Ramirez and Oakley.
Reversed: paragraph 9 says the skin contains the same opsin found in the retina.
Reversed: paragraph 9 says the skin uses the one pigment the eye uses and cannot by itself add color discrimination.
Reversed: paragraph 9 says the response is slow, taking seconds.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Cephalopods change color by means of hormones acting on single pigment cells, in much the same way that fish and frogs change theirs
The Stubbs hypothesis has settled the question of how color-blind cephalopods manage to see color
Cephalopod skin contains three kinds of cells, and the leucophore is the most important of them for camouflage
Cephalopod color change is a fast, well-understood neural system, but how a color-blind animal matches colors is still unresolved
Because cephalopods have only a single visual pigment, their camouflage cannot genuinely match the colors of their surroundings

proof.quote: a cuttlefish can switch its entire body pattern in under a second
yet the eyes that direct it appear to be color-blind
The rest, the question of how a color-blind animal paints itself to suit a colored world, is open

questions.why: The first half of the passage explains the fast, nerve-driven machinery of the skin; the second half sets out a puzzle, that the eyes directing it appear color-blind, and weighs three explanations without settling on one. Paragraph 10 says plainly what is certain and what is still open.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraphs 2 and 3 say the cephalopod system is muscular and neural, with no hormone in the loop, unlike the vertebrate cell.
Contradicted: paragraph 8 says the hypothesis remains a calculation that no one has yet demonstrated.
Too narrow and unsupported: the three cell types are one part of the passage, and the author never ranks the leucophore first.
Too strong: paragraph 7 says spectral measurements found the match good but not perfect, and the author treats the question as open rather than closed.
